candidate.answerReason: Every feasible configuration has at least 19 blue chips and therefore at least 57 red chips. A configuration with 36 white, 19 blue, and 57 red chips attains this bound.

methods.label: Bound the blue count, then attain the red bound
methods.explanation:
Let \(W,B,R\) be the nonnegative integer counts of white, blue, and red chips. The conditions give
\[
W\le2B,\qquad R\ge3B,\qquad W+B\ge55.
\]
To make the red count small, first find how small the blue count can be. Since the white count is at most twice the blue count,
\[
55\le W+B\le3B.
\]
Thus \(B\ge55/3\). Because chips come in whole numbers, \(B\ge19\), so
\[
R\ge3B\ge57.
\]

A lower bound is a minimum only if it can be attained. Take \(W=36\), \(B=19\), and \(R=57\). Then \(19\ge36/2\), \(19=57/3\), and \(36+19=55\), so every condition holds. Therefore the minimum red count is \(\boxed{57}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary linear inequalities, integer restrictions, and a direct construction attaining the bound.

candidate.annotationRationale: Modeling simultaneous chip restrictions is an application of systems of inequalities. Proving the minimum requires both a universal bound and a feasible configuration attaining it. Verbal inequality translation and inequality properties support the method; a general procedure for solving one-variable inequality systems is not used.

review.mathematicalCheck: The constraints imply 55≤W+B≤3B, so integer B≥19 and R≥57. The counts W=36, B=19, R=57 satisfy every condition and attain the bound.
